title: A Voice in the Wilderness
sum: Luke dates the start of the story like a historian: the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, Annas and Caiaphas in office. Into that world comes a word from God to John, Zechariah's son, in the wilderness. He preaches a baptism of repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's voice that prepares the Lord's road so that all flesh will see God's salvation. He warns the crowds that being Abraham's children will not save them, and when they ask, "What are we to do?" he gives plain answers: share clothes and food, collect only what is owed, stop extorting.

When people wonder whether John is the Messiah, he points to a stronger one who will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire. Luke then closes John's story with his imprisonment by Herod, before telling, in a single sentence, how Jesus was baptized among the people and, while praying, received the Spirit in bodily shape and heard the Father's voice. A genealogy follows, running from Jesus back through David and Abraham to Adam and to God.
readings: Luke anchors the gospel in public history. His list of rulers can be checked, and most of it fits what Josephus and inscriptions tell us: Pilate's title, the dates of Antipas and Philip, the joint mention of Annas and Caiaphas. Josephus also confirms John's preaching, his popularity and his death at Herod's hands, though he describes the baptism in moral rather than end-of-the-world terms. Historians of every background accept that Jesus was baptized by John, if only because the early church would not have invented a story that seemed to place Jesus below John.

Luke builds the chapter to introduce Jesus. John's preaching ends on "all flesh will see God's salvation," so the story is for the whole world. John's ethics (sharing, honesty, no violence) preview Jesus' teaching on wealth and power. John leaves the stage before Jesus is baptized. The Spirit comes while Jesus prays. And the genealogy runs to Adam, "son of God," just before the devil says, "If you are God's Son." Read this way, each piece points forward to the Gospel and to Acts.

views.H: The fifteenth year of Tiberius is about AD 28–29. Pontius Pilate (prefect 26–36), Herod Antipas (tetrarch 4 BC–AD 39) and Philip (4 BC–AD 34) are well attested. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15 and Caiaphas held office from about 18 to 36. Josephus describes John as a good man who called Jews to justice and piety and baptized them, and says Antipas executed him at Machaerus for fear his influence would lead to revolt (Antiquities 18.116–119). The tax contractors and soldiers of the chapter fit early Roman Galilee and Judea.
views.C: Luke follows Mark's outline (John, baptism, testing) and shares with Matthew the speech of 3:7–9 and 3:16–17, usually assigned to the common source Q; 3:10–14 is Luke's own material. Luke moves John's arrest before the baptism, perhaps to separate the two figures (Conzelmann) or simply to finish John's story. The genealogy differs from Matthew's between David and Joseph; most critical scholars think neither list can be shown to be historical record, and that each served its writer's theology. The Western reading at 3:22 (Psalm 2:7) has been argued as original by some, notably Ehrman, but most text critics reject it.
views.L: The chapter is a carefully built transition. A long, formal sentence (3:1–2) moves the story from the temple world of chapters 1–2 into the wilderness and the Roman world. John's preaching follows a pattern Luke loves: warning, question ("What are we to do?"), concrete answer. The one-sentence baptism places the emphasis on what follows it: prayer, the opened heaven, the Spirit, the voice. The genealogy is placed not at the start of the book, as in Matthew, but at the start of Jesus' public life, between "You are my dearly loved Son" and "If you are God's Son."
views.J: John's message is an inner-Jewish prophetic call, in the line of Amos and Jeremiah, to the children of Abraham. His washing resembles Jewish purity rites, and Qumran's community also took Isaiah 40:3 as its charter in the desert. His warning about trusting descent from Abraham was later used by Christians to argue that Jews had been replaced, but John's point, like the prophets', is that God expects the fruit of a changed life from his own people. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine note that tax collectors and soldiers come to a Jewish prophet for guidance and are told to stay in their work and act justly.
views.T: The Eastern churches celebrate Jesus' baptism at Theophany (January 6) as the revealing of the Trinity, and bless water on that day; the Western church keeps the Baptism of the Lord after Epiphany. Luke 3:14 became a key text in Christian thinking about military service from Augustine on (see the card). The genealogy is read in some Western churches before Christmas or on Epiphany. Medieval art often painted John as the last prophet of the Old Testament and the first witness of the New.

deep.b:
Luke 3:1–2 is the most detailed date in the Gospels: an emperor, a governor, three tetrarchs and two high priests, then a prophet. The emperor and his governor stand for Rome; the tetrarchs for the Herodian princes who ruled for Rome; the high priests for the temple aristocracy. Each of these powers reappears in Luke's account of Jesus' death: Pilate and Herod judge him (23:1–25), and the chief priests press the charges (22:66–71).

Against them all, "a word from God came to" John, not in a palace or the temple but in the wilderness. Luke's readers would hear the opening lines of Jeremiah, Hosea and the other prophets, which also date God's word by the reign of kings (Jeremiah 1:1–3; Hosea 1:1). The structure makes a claim: the decisive event of the age is happening on the edge of the empire, among people its rulers hardly noticed.

Luke's genealogy runs upward from Jesus through 77 names to Adam, and then to God; Matthew's runs downward from Abraham to Jesus in three sets of fourteen (Matthew 1:1–17). From Abraham to David the lists agree (with small differences of spelling and the names Admin and Arni; see the variants). From David to Joseph they share only Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. Matthew goes through Solomon and the kings of Judah; Luke through Nathan and private names unknown elsewhere. Matthew makes Joseph's father Jacob; Luke, Heli. Codex Bezae goes its own way: from Joseph back to David it replaces Luke's names with Matthew's line in reverse order, with some additions (as reported by Metzger). It also reads "Aram" at 3:33, as Matthew 1:3–4 does, and leaves out the second Cainan at 3:36, who is missing from the Hebrew of Genesis 11 (see the variants).

Four main explanations have been offered. (1) Levirate marriage: Julius Africanus, in a letter quoted by Eusebius (Church History 1.7), said he had it from the family of Jesus that Jacob and Heli were half-brothers with the same mother; when Heli died childless, Jacob married his widow, so Joseph was Jacob's son by birth and Heli's by law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). (2) Mary's line: from the late Middle Ages many, especially Protestants, have read Luke's list as Mary's, with Heli as her father; supporters note that Luke tells the birth from Mary's side and qualifies Joseph's fatherhood ("people supposed"), while critics answer that Luke's grammar runs the line through Joseph and that Jewish genealogies were traced through men. (3) Royal and natural lines: Matthew gives the line of legal heirs to David's throne, Luke the actual descent. (4) Theological construction: most critical scholars, such as Raymond Brown and Marshall Johnson, think the lists came from different traditions or were built for theological purposes: Matthew to show Jesus as son of David and Abraham, Luke to show him as son of Adam and of God; their history can no longer be tested.

All four Gospels and Paul agree that Jesus was of David's line (Romans 1:3), and early Jewish opponents did not, so far as we know, dispute it. Hegesippus reports that the emperor Domitian questioned relatives of Jesus as descendants of David (Eusebius, Church History 3.20).

In the critical text Luke's list has 77 names from Adam to Jesus (78 if God is counted). Richard Bauckham (Jude and the Relatives of Jesus, 1990) has proposed that the number is deliberate: in 1 Enoch 10:12 the fallen angels are bound "for seventy generations" until the judgment, counted from Enoch, who is seventh from Adam (Jude 1:14). Counted from Adam, Luke's list puts Enoch seventh and Jesus seventy-seventh, at the end of the eleventh group of seven generations, so the twelfth and last age of world history, in some Jewish schemes, begins with him. Bauckham suggests the list came from Jesus' relatives, who are known to have valued their Davidic descent. Other scholars think the count is accidental, since the manuscripts differ on several names (3:33; 3:36). The suggestion is a proposal, not a consensus.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a body at the start and at the end
deep.b: Only Luke says the Spirit came down "in bodily shape" (3:22). Only Luke has the risen Jesus insist that he is not a spirit but has flesh and bones, and eat fish in front of his disciples (24:39–43). I suggest the two are a deliberate frame: Luke opens Jesus' public life with the invisible Spirit made visible in bodily form and closes it with the risen Jesus proving he is not a spirit but has a body. Between them, the genealogy roots Jesus in a physical human family back to Adam. The frame would answer any reader inclined to think spiritual things cannot be bodily, or that Jesus only seemed human. This overlaps with the common scholarly view that Luke stresses the reality of Jesus' body against early docetic ideas (for example Charles Talbert), but the specific pairing of 3:22 and 24:39 as a frame is my own suggestion.

echoes: Isaiah 40:3–5; Jeremiah 1:1–3; Hosea 1:1; Malachi 3:1–3; Isaiah 51:1–2; Leviticus 18:16; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 5:1–32; Genesis 11:10–26; 1 Chronicles 1:1–34; 1 Chronicles 2:1–15; Ruth 4:18–22; Matthew 3:1–17; Matthew 1:1–17; Mark 1:1–11; Mark 6:17–29; John 1:19–34; Acts 1:5; Acts 13:24–25; Acts 19:1–7

traditions.q: John did not tell the soldiers to leave the army, only to stop extorting and be content with their pay (3:14). Does that show a Christian may serve as a soldier? (The wider question of force and war is on the card at Matthew 5:39.)
views: Yes. Augustine argued that if Christian teaching condemned all wars, John would have told the soldiers to throw away their arms; instead he told them to do no violence and be content with their pay (Letter 138, to Marcellinus). Thomas Aquinas repeats the argument in defending just war (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 40, article 1). The Catechism calls those in military service servants of the security and freedom of nations (Catechism 2310).

The church honors soldier saints such as George, Demetrius and Theodore, and does not forbid military service. Yet killing is never treated as simply innocent: Basil the Great advised that soldiers who killed in war refrain from communion for three years (Letter 188, canon 13).

Yes. Christians may "serve as soldiers" (Augsburg Confession, article 16). Luther, in Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved, appeals to John's answer as approving the soldier's calling, so long as it serves justice and peace.
Yes. Calvin repeats Augustine's reasoning from this verse: had God wished to forbid soldiering, John would have said so (Institutes 4.20.12).

No. John spoke before Jesus taught his disciples to love their enemies (6:27–36), and he told the soldiers only to stop abusing their power. The sword is "outside the perfection of Christ" (Schleitheim Confession, article 6), and Mennonites and other peace churches refuse military service. Tertullian had already answered the appeal to John's soldiers: in disarming Peter, the Lord "unbelted every soldier" (On Idolatry 19).

settings.what: Isaiah's voice in the wilderness
settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: As John begins preaching by the Jordan
settings.why: To show that John's work is the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that God would come back to his people, and to stretch the promise to the whole world: "all flesh will see God's salvation." Matthew and Mark quote only the first line; Luke's longer quotation tells readers from the start that the gospel is meant for Gentiles as well as Jews.
settings.readers: For Luke's mostly Gentile Christian readers, perhaps including Theophilus, the quotation said that they were part of God's plan from the beginning, not latecomers.

settings.what: John's warning to the crowds
settings.to: The crowds coming out to the Jordan to be baptized: ordinary Jews from Judea and the surrounding region
settings.when: During John's preaching in the wilderness, in the late 20s AD
settings.why: To shake people who thought that coming for the rite, or being descended from Abraham, would protect them from God's coming judgment. John demands a changed life ("fruits worthy of repentance") and warns that judgment is already at the root of the tree. In Matthew the same words are aimed at Pharisees and Sadducees; in Luke at everyone, so no one in the audience can assume the warning is for someone else.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, baptized Christians, would hear that baptism without a changed life is not enough, a theme Luke repeats (6:46; 13:25–27).

settings.what: John's answers to three groups
settings.to: First the crowds, then tax collectors, then men serving as soldiers, each asking, "What are we to do?"
settings.when: At the Jordan, after his warning
settings.why: To make repentance concrete in daily life. The crowds are told to share their spare tunic and food; tax collectors to collect only the official amount; soldiers to stop extorting by force or false charges and to live on their pay. John does not tell anyone to leave home or job, but to stop using their position to take from others. The two groups most despised for exploiting the poor are told to stop exploiting.
settings.readers: Luke's church included people of means, officials and probably soldiers (Acts 10). The passage gave them a standard for living out faith in the jobs they had, and prepared for Luke's many teachings on wealth.

settings.what: John's promise of the stronger one
settings.to: All the people, who were wondering whether John himself might be the Messiah
settings.when: At the height of John's popularity
settings.why: To turn the people's hopes away from himself to a greater figure who would baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire and would sort the wheat from the chaff. John places himself below a slave of the coming one. For hearers who expected a Messiah, the words promised that he was near and that his coming would both cleanse and judge. Matthew (3:11–12) and Mark (1:7–8) give the saying without the people's question; in John (1:19–27) a delegation from Jerusalem asks John who he is.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew the fulfillment: the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4). Any who still honored John too highly (Acts 18:24–19:7) were reminded of John's own words.

settings.what: The voice from heaven
settings.to: Jesus himself ("You are"), while he prays after his baptism among the people
settings.when: Just after Jesus' baptism, as the Spirit comes down on him
settings.why: To confirm Jesus as God's beloved Son and Spirit-anointed servant at the start of his public work, in words drawn from Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 42:1 and Genesis 22:2. In Luke the voice addresses Jesus personally; it is a word of identity and commission before the testing in the wilderness. In Matthew the voice speaks about him ("This is my dearly loved Son," Matthew 3:17); in Mark and Luke it speaks to him.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, the scene is the anointing that Jesus will claim in Nazareth (4:18) and that Peter will preach in Acts 10:38.

settings.what: Jesus' family line
settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: Placed between the baptism and the testing, as Jesus begins his work at about thirty
settings.why: To show who Jesus is by descent: son of David (through Nathan), son of Abraham, son of Adam, and so son of God. Luke's list runs upward to God, linking the voice at the baptism ("You are my dearly loved Son") with the devil's taunt ("If you are God's Son") and presenting Jesus as one who belongs to all humanity, not only to Israel.
settings.readers: For Gentile believers the list said that the Messiah of Israel is also the descendant of the ancestor of every nation, and that God's plan includes them.
views: Many read the list as Joseph's, giving Jesus his legal descent as Joseph's adopted son.
Others read it as Mary's, with Heli as her father; see the chapter's deep section.

title: Today This Scripture Is Fulfilled
sum: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led through the wilderness for forty days and tested by the devil. Hungry, he refuses to turn a stone into bread; offered all the kingdoms of the world for a bow, he refuses; set on the temple's high corner in Jerusalem and urged to throw himself down on the strength of a psalm, he refuses again. Each answer comes from Deuteronomy, from Moses' words about Israel's forty years. The devil leaves him until another time.

Back in Galilee in the Spirit's power, Jesus teaches in synagogues. In Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61, announces good news to the poor and release to captives, and says, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled." Admiration turns to anger when he reminds his hometown that Elijah and Elisha were sent to foreigners, and the crowd tries to throw him off a cliff, but he walks away. In Capernaum he teaches with authority, drives out a demon, heals Simon's mother-in-law of a fever and many others at sunset, and then moves on to preach the kingdom of God in other towns.
readings: Many scholars call the Nazareth scene (4:16–30) Luke's "inaugural address": in a few verses it sets out the whole Gospel and Acts. The Spirit anoints Jesus; he brings good news to the poor, release and healing; he is rejected by his own; God's care reaches outsiders; and he passes through death's threat and goes on his way. The healings that follow in Capernaum show the program at work: release from demons and sickness.

The testing retells Israel's forty years in the wilderness in Jesus' forty days. Israel was hungry and grumbled, was tempted by other gods, and put God to the test at Massah; Jesus, quoting Moses' sermon about those years (Deuteronomy 6–8), trusts God for food, worships God alone, and refuses to force God's hand. Read this way, Jesus is the faithful Son that Israel was called to be (Exodus 4:22), and his answers are a model for any believer under pressure.

views.H: Nazareth was a small Jewish village in lower Galilee, Capernaum a fishing town on the lake near the border of Antipas' territory. First-century synagogue buildings have been found at Magdala and Gamla, and later Jewish sources describe readings from the Law and the Prophets. That Jesus was a healer and exorcist is accepted by historians of every background, whatever they think was happening. The location of the temple's "high corner" and of Nazareth's cliff are uncertain.
views.C: Luke follows Mark in the order of the Capernaum day (4:31–44 = Mark 1:21–39), but places the Nazareth rejection, which Mark tells later (Mark 6:1–6), at the head of Jesus' work and expands it greatly. 4:23 refers to deeds in Capernaum not yet told, which suggests the move. The testing narrative is shared with Matthew (from Q, or from Matthew on the Farrer view), with the second and third tests in a different order. Luke's Isaiah quotation follows the Septuagint and joins Isaiah 58:6 to 61:1–2, which some think is Luke's work, others a pre-Lukan or synagogue practice.
views.L: Luke links the scenes by the Spirit (4:1, 14, 18) and by "God's Son" (3:22, 38; 4:3, 9, 41). The devil leaves "until his next chance" (4:13), which points to the Passion (22:3, 53). In Nazareth admiration turns to rage within a few verses, a pattern repeated in Acts. Wordplay ties the sermon together: the "year of the Lord's welcome" (4:19) and "no prophet is welcome" (4:24). Jesus' escape (4:30) and his "I must" (4:43) show his journey moving forward by God's plan.
views.J: Jesus is pictured as a Jew at home in synagogue life: at the synagogue every Sabbath, reading the Prophets, teaching, healing after sunset when the Sabbath ends. His examples of Elijah and Elisha come from Israel's own Scriptures and from prophets who rebuked Israel from within. 11QMelchizedek and 4Q521 show that Isaiah 61 was read in Jesus' time as a promise of release and healing in the last days. Readers should not take one village's anger as a picture of "the Jews"; Luke goes on to show crowds of Jews welcoming Jesus.
views.T: The Western church reads the testing on the First Sunday of Lent, in memory of Jesus' forty days (see the card at Matthew 4:2). Luke 4:18–19 is the classic text for the church's mission to the poor, from medieval preaching to modern Catholic social teaching and liberation theology; John Paul II used it to call for the Jubilee of 2000. Many churches read it at ordinations as the pattern of Christian ministry.

deep.h: The three tests in Matthew and Luke
deep.b:
Matthew and Luke share the dialogue almost word for word, but Luke has a different order for the second and third tests:

Matthew 4:1–11: stones to bread; the temple in the holy city; the high mountain and the kingdoms; ends with "Go away, Satan!" and angels serving him.

Luke 4:1–13: stone to bread; the kingdoms of the inhabited world, shown "in a split second"; Jerusalem and the temple; ends with the devil leaving "until his next chance."

Matthew's order rises to a mountain, where his Gospel also ends (Matthew 28:16–20). Luke's ends in Jerusalem, the goal of Jesus' journey (9:51) and the city where the devil will return through Judas (22:3). Most scholars think Luke changed the order; some think Matthew did. Jesus' three answers all come from Moses' sermon about Israel's testing in the wilderness. In Matthew they run backward through it (Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:16, 6:13); Luke's order (8:3, 6:13, 6:16) breaks that pattern, which is one argument that Matthew kept the source's order. Both Gospels thus present Jesus as the faithful Son who passes the tests Israel failed.

deep.h: The Nazareth sermon as Luke's program
deep.b:
Luke's scene in Nazareth is longer and earlier than Mark's (Mark 6:1–6) and works as a summary of the whole story. The Spirit: Jesus reads, "The Spirit of the Lord is on me," right after the Spirit has come down at his baptism; in Acts the same Spirit is poured on the church (Acts 2:17–18). Good news to the poor and release: the healings, exorcisms and forgiveness that follow are that release, as Jesus tells John's disciples (7:22). Today: the promises are not postponed. Rejection by his own and care for outsiders: the widow of Zarephath and Naaman anticipate the centurion (7:1–10), the Samaritan (10:30–37; 17:16) and the Gentile mission of Acts, where Paul's preaching is often welcomed and then violently opposed in the synagogues (Acts 13:44–50). Escape from death: led to a height to be killed, Jesus "passed through the middle of them and kept going," a preview of the cross and resurrection.

The scene also shows what is left out. Jesus stops before "a day of our God's vengeance" (Isaiah 61:2). Christians have read this as the difference between his first and second comings; others see it as the character of his message, which offers mercy first.

Jesus' reading was not a random choice. Isaiah 61 was read in his time as a promise of the last days. In 11QMelchizedek, a Dead Sea Scroll from the first century BC, Isaiah 61 is combined with the jubilee laws of Leviticus 25 and with Isaiah 52:7: a heavenly figure, Melchizedek, will proclaim release to the captives in the tenth and last jubilee, atone for the sons of light and execute God's vengeance. In 4Q521, sometimes called the "Messianic Apocalypse," the heavens and earth will listen to God's anointed one, and the Lord will free captives, give sight to the blind, heal the wounded, give life to the dead and "proclaim good news to the poor." The last phrase is the same combination Jesus uses when John's disciples ask if he is the one to come (7:22).

These texts show that Jesus' hearers could understand Isaiah 61 as the announcement of God's final act of liberation. Jesus' claim, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled," put him in that role.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Nazareth as the Passion in miniature
deep.b: Luke 4:16–30 does not only preview the Gospel's themes; it seems to me to trace the order of its final chapters. Jesus is welcomed with praise (4:22; compare the entry into Jerusalem, 19:37–38); his claim provokes his own people (4:28; compare 22:70–71); they "rose up" and "threw him out" of the town (4:29; the crucifixion took place outside the city, and Luke uses the same verb for throwing the son out of the vineyard, 20:15); they lead him to a height to kill him (4:29); and he "passed through the middle of them and kept going" (4:30), as the risen Jesus appears among the disciples and then is taken up (24:36, 51). The overlap with published scholarship is large, since many scholars, including Robert Tannehill, read 4:16–30 as foreshadowing the Passion; the point-by-point sequence, including the verb of 20:15, is my own reading.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:13; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 91:11–12; Isaiah 61:1–2; Isaiah 58:6; Leviticus 25:8–13; 1 Kings 17:8–24; 1 Kings 18:1; 2 Kings 5:1–14; Matthew 4:1–17; Matthew 13:53–58; Mark 1:12–15; Mark 1:21–39; Mark 6:1–6; John 4:44; John 6:42; Acts 10:38; Acts 13:44–50

settings.what: The devil's three tests and Jesus' answers
settings.by: The devil, and Jesus answering from Deuteronomy
settings.to: Each other, alone in the wilderness and then in Jerusalem
settings.when: During and at the end of forty days in the wilderness, right after the baptism
settings.why: The devil tries to turn Jesus' sonship toward self-help (bread), power by compromise (the kingdoms) and a forced display of God's care (the temple leap). Jesus answers each time with Moses' words to Israel about its testing in the wilderness, choosing trust, worship of God alone and refusal to test God. The scene shows what kind of Son and Messiah he will be before he begins. Matthew (4:1–11) has the temple test second and the kingdoms, seen from a very high mountain, last.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who faced pressure to compromise with Rome's power and the worship around them, were given Jesus' answers as their own. The offer of "every kingdom of the inhabited world" would sound like the empire itself.

settings.what: The reading from Isaiah and the sermon in Nazareth
settings.to: The Sabbath congregation in the synagogue at Nazareth, his hometown: neighbors and relatives who had watched him grow up
settings.when: Early in his work in Galilee, after reports from elsewhere had spread
settings.why: To announce, with Isaiah 61:1–2 and 58:6, that the Spirit-anointed messenger of God's release has come, and that the promise is being fulfilled "today" in their hearing. For villagers under Herod's taxes and Rome's rule, "release to the captives" and "a year of the Lord's welcome" would sound like the jubilee and the end of their troubles. Knowing the audience explains the turn: they expected the benefits to start at home. Mark (6:1–6) and Matthew (13:53–58) tell the Nazareth visit later in Jesus' work, without the reading from Isaiah.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the sermon is Jesus' own summary of his mission, to be continued by the church in the power of the same Spirit (Acts 1:8; 10:38).

settings.what: A prophet not welcome at home
settings.to: The same Nazareth congregation, as their admiration turns to suspicion
settings.when: Right after the reading, when they ask, "This is Joseph's son, isn't it?"
settings.why: To answer their unspoken demand for miracles at home ("Doctor, cure yourself") and to warn them that God's prophets are not owned by their hometown. Jesus uses Israel's own Scriptures: Elijah fed and raised the son of a widow in Sidon, and Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian, when Israel had many in need. The examples tell a village that wanted favors that God's mercy goes where God sends it, even to outsiders.
settings.readers: Luke's mixed Jewish and Gentile churches would hear the story of their own origins: the message going to the nations, as in Acts 13:46–48 and 28:28. The warning is against claiming God's favor as a possession, not a verdict on the Jewish people.

settings.what: The demon's cry and Jesus' command
settings.by: An unclean demon speaking through a man, then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus, and then the demon, before the Sabbath congregation in Capernaum
settings.when: During Jesus' Sabbath teaching in the Capernaum synagogue
settings.why: The demon tries to gain control by naming Jesus ("the Holy One of God") and asks whether he has come to destroy "us." Jesus silences it and drives it out with a word. For the congregation, the event shows that his teaching carries authority over evil powers, and they ask, "What is this message?"
settings.readers: For Luke's readers in a world full of spirits, magic and fear of demons, the story showed that Jesus' word frees people without spells or rituals, as the apostles' word does in Acts (Acts 16:16–18; 19:11–20).

settings.what: "I must tell the other towns the good news"
settings.to: The crowds from Capernaum who had come after him to a deserted place and tried to keep him
settings.when: At daybreak, after a night of healing
settings.why: To explain why he will not settle in one successful place: he was sent to announce the kingdom of God in every town. After Nazareth tried to throw him out and Capernaum tries to hold him back, Jesus makes clear that neither rejection nor popularity sets his course; God's purpose does. In Mark (1:35–38) it is Simon and the others who come after him, and Jesus says he came out to preach in the neighboring towns.
settings.readers: For the church in Acts, which also had to keep moving "as far as the farthest end of the earth" (Acts 1:8), Jesus' "I must" gave the pattern.

title: From Now On You Will Catch People
sum: By the Lake of Gennesaret Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells him to let down the nets in deep water. After a fruitless night, Simon obeys, and the catch is so large that two boats begin to sink. Simon falls at Jesus' knees, confessing he is a sinful man, and Jesus tells him not to be afraid: from now on he will be catching people alive. Simon, James and John leave everything and follow him. Jesus touches and cleanses a man full of skin disease and sends him to the priest, and his fame spreads while he withdraws to pray.

Then come the first disputes. Pharisees and teachers of the law watch as friends lower a paralyzed man through a tiled roof; Jesus declares his sins forgiven and, when the scribes cry blasphemy, heals him to show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. He calls Levi the tax collector, eats at his banquet with tax collectors and sinners, and answers the complaints: the sick need a doctor; he came to call sinners to repentance. Asked why his disciples feast instead of fasting, he speaks of a groom, a patch, new wine and old.
readings: The catch of fish follows the pattern of prophetic calls: a sign of divine power, the called person's fear and sense of unworthiness (like Isaiah's "Woe to me!"), reassurance, a commission and obedience. Luke places it after Simon has seen Jesus heal in his own home, so his response is grounded. Levi's call (5:27–28) repeats the pattern in brief, and both men "leave everything."

From 5:17 to 6:11 Luke, following Mark, sets five scenes of conflict: forgiveness, eating with sinners, fasting, plucking grain on the Sabbath and healing on the Sabbath. In each, Jesus' actions raise a question about authority and the Law, and he answers with a short, memorable saying. Read this way, the chapter shows the new thing Jesus brings (the groom is here; new wine needs new skins) and the resistance it meets, while Luke's closing saying, "The old is good," admits the pull of the familiar.

views.H: Fishing on the Lake of Galilee was a family business organized in partnerships, as the boat found near Magdala in 1986 illustrates. Capernaum lay near a border and had a customs post. Houses there had flat roofs of beams and mud reached by outside stairs; Luke's "tiles" describe a roof familiar to his readers. Pharisees were active in Galilee, though their numbers and influence there are debated. Tax collectors were disliked as collaborators and cheats.
views.C: Luke 5:1–11 replaces Mark's short call story (Mark 1:16–20) with a longer account of a miraculous catch, closely similar to John 21:1–11; many scholars think both go back to one tradition, perhaps originally a resurrection appearance. From 5:12 Luke follows Mark 1:40–2:22 closely, smoothing the Greek, omitting the healed man's disobedience (Mark 1:45) and adding characteristic touches: Jesus' habit of prayer (5:16), "to repentance" (5:32), "and prayers" (5:33) and the saying about old wine (5:39).
views.L: The chapter moves from water to roof to banquet table. Simon's words progress from "Master" to "Lord." "Today" (5:26) echoes Nazareth (4:21). The word "forgive" (5:20–24) picks up the "release" of 4:18. The images at the end (groom, garment, wine) gather the themes of joy and newness, and the final line holds the new and the old in tension.
views.J: Jesus sends the cleansed man to the priest with the offering the Law requires (Leviticus 14), showing respect for the Torah. The scribes' question "Who is able to forgive sins except God alone?" is a sound Jewish theological point. The Pharisees appear as serious observers who come "from every village," and the disputes are internal debates about how to be faithful. Fasting and prayer were marks of Jewish piety that Jesus does not reject; he says his disciples will fast. Luke 5:39, "The old is good," has been read as a respectful word about Jewish tradition.
views.T: The miraculous catch and "catching people" became a classic image of the church's mission; the fish (Greek ichthys) was an early Christian symbol. Catholic and Orthodox teaching links 5:20–24 with the church's ministry of forgiveness in confession (see the cards at Matthew 9 and Psalm 32). The saying about fasting "when the groom is taken away" supported the church's fast days (see the card at Matthew 6:16). Monastic tradition read "they left it all" as a call to religious poverty.

deep.h: The catch in Luke 5 and in John 21
deep.b:
The two stories share an unusual number of details:

Both: fishermen have worked all night and caught nothing; Jesus tells them where to let down the net; the catch is enormous; the net is under strain; Simon Peter reacts dramatically (falling at Jesus' knees in Luke; jumping into the sea in John); the scene ends with a commission to Peter.

Differences: Luke's story is at the start of Jesus' work, John's after the resurrection; in Luke Jesus is in the boat, in John on the shore; in Luke the nets begin to tear, in John "still the net did not tear" (John 21:11); Luke's commission is "catching people," John's "feed my sheep."

Many traditional interpreters see two events, with the second meant to recall the first as Peter is restored after his denials. Many critical scholars, such as Raymond Brown and Joseph Fitzmyer, think a single tradition stands behind both, most likely a resurrection appearance to Peter (compare 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5) that Luke placed in the ministry. Either way, Luke makes Peter's call the story of a sinful man commissioned by grace, which fits the Peter who will later deny Jesus and be restored (22:31–34, 61–62).

Following Mark 2:1–3:6, Luke groups five scenes in which Jesus' actions are questioned: forgiving sins (5:17–26), eating with tax collectors and sinners (5:27–32), not fasting (5:33–39), plucking grain on the Sabbath (6:1–5) and healing on the Sabbath (6:6–11). Joanna Dewey has argued that Mark arranged them in a ring, with the fasting saying, and its hint of the groom "taken away," at the center. Luke keeps the series but softens the ending: where Mark has the Pharisees plotting with the Herodians to destroy Jesus (Mark 3:6), Luke has them only discussing among themselves what to do about him (6:11).

Each debate turns on authority. The Son of Man has authority to forgive sins on earth (5:24) and is Lord of the Sabbath (6:5); the doctor goes to the sick (5:31); the groom's presence changes the calendar (5:34). The opponents are not villains but representatives of serious Jewish piety asking reasonable questions, which is what makes Jesus' answers matter.

Only Luke adds 5:39 to the sayings about new wine. It seems to undercut them, which is probably why Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies leave it out. Interpreters have read it in three ways. Most take it as irony: those who are content with the old will not even taste the new, and that explains the rejection Jesus meets. Some take it as Luke's respect for the old: Luke-Acts honors the Law, the temple and Jewish piety (1:6; 2:22–24; Acts 21:20–26), and the saying warns the church against despising its Jewish roots. Others see a simple proverb about taste, like Sirach's comparison of a new friend to new wine that becomes pleasant only with age (Sirach 9:10).

The saying may hold more than one of these at once. Luke's story is about something new that is also the fulfillment of the old, and about people who find it hard to let go of what they know.

echoes: Isaiah 6:1–8; Jeremiah 16:16; Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; 2 Kings 5:14; Isaiah 43:25; 2 Samuel 12:13; Daniel 7:13–14; Hosea 6:6; Isaiah 62:5; Isaiah 53:8; Matthew 4:18–22; Matthew 8:1–4; Matthew 9:1–17; Mark 1:16–20; Mark 1:40–2:22; John 21:1–19; Acts 2:38

settings.what: The command to fish and the call of Simon
settings.to: Simon, the owner of the boat, and through him his partners James and John
settings.when: After Jesus had taught the crowds from Simon's boat on the Lake of Gennesaret, following a night in which the fishermen caught nothing
settings.why: To show Simon, a professional fisherman who had already seen Jesus heal in his own house, what obeying Jesus' word produces, and then to give him a new task. Simon's fear ("I am a sinful man") is answered with "Stop being afraid" and a commission to catch people alive. The command aimed at Simon's trade and pride, then gave it a new purpose. Mark (1:16–20) and Matthew (4:18–22) tell the call by the shore, with no catch and before any healing in Simon's house.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew Peter as the leader of the first church (Acts 1–12). The story told them that his authority rested on grace given to a man who confessed he was a sinner, and that their own mission continued his catch.

settings.what: The cleansing and the order to go to the priest
settings.by: A man full of skin disease, then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus; then the healed man
settings.when: In one of the Galilean towns
settings.why: The man asks not for healing but for cleanness: "you are able to make me clean." Jesus touches him, cleanses him, and then sends him to the priest to make the offerings of Leviticus 14. The order binds the healed man, and through him the priests at the temple in Jerusalem, who alone could declare him clean and restore him to worship and community. Jesus works within the Law's procedure, so that the man's return is official and the priests themselves receive the evidence.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the scene shows Jesus as one who keeps the Law and restores outcasts to community, a pattern Luke repeats with the ten men in 17:11–19.

settings.what: Forgiveness declared and defended
settings.to: First the paralyzed man; then the scribes and Pharisees who were reasoning in their hearts
settings.when: While Jesus taught in a crowded house, with Pharisees and teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem present
settings.why: To meet the man's deepest need first, and then to answer the experts' objection that only God forgives sins. Jesus does not deny their principle; he gives a visible sign (the healing) for an invisible claim (authority to forgive). For teachers who had come to assess him, the scene presented the choice between blasphemy and a new act of God.
settings.readers: Luke's church proclaimed "forgiveness of sins" in Jesus' name (24:47; Acts 2:38; 13:38). The story grounded that message in Jesus' own authority on earth.

settings.what: "Follow me"
settings.to: Levi, a tax collector at his booth in Capernaum
settings.when: As Jesus went out after the healing of the paralyzed man
settings.why: To call into his close company a man whose work made him despised as a collaborator and a cheat. The call comes without conditions, and Levi leaves everything. Coming right after the declaration of forgiveness, it shows what forgiveness means in practice. Matthew (9:9) calls the tax collector Matthew.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, among whom were people with questionable pasts and with money, saw that Jesus' call reached them too, and what answering it required.

settings.what: The complaint about eating with sinners and Jesus' reply
settings.by: The Pharisees and their scribes, then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus' disciples (the complaint); then the critics (Jesus' answer)
settings.when: At Levi's large banquet for tax collectors and others
settings.why: The critics, who kept careful purity and table rules, objected to sharing food with known lawbreakers, which in their culture meant accepting them. Jesus answers with a doctor's logic: healers go to the sick. He has come to call sinners to repentance. The saying defends his table fellowship without denying that sin is real.
settings.readers: For a church where Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor, upright and notorious sat at one table (Acts 10–11; 15), Jesus' words justified their mixed meals and their mission to outsiders.

settings.what: The question about fasting
settings.by: Critics (in Luke apparently the same Pharisees and scribes), then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus
settings.when: At or after Levi's banquet
settings.why: The questioners contrast the disciples of John and of the Pharisees, who fast and pray often, with Jesus' disciples who feast. Jesus answers that wedding guests do not fast while the groom is present, but the groom will be taken away, and then they will fast. The answer claims that his presence is a time of joy like a wedding, and hints at his coming death. In Mark (2:18) unnamed people ask; in Matthew (9:14) John's disciples ask for themselves.
settings.readers: Luke's readers fasted (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). The saying explained why: the groom had been taken away, and they waited for him.

settings.what: Parable of the patch
settings.to: The same critics
settings.when: Continuing the answer about fasting
settings.why: To show that the new thing Jesus brings cannot be cut up to repair the old pattern of piety: the new is ruined and the old not helped. For critics who wanted Jesus' disciples to fit existing customs, the parable said the new way needs its own form. Luke's version (a patch torn from a new coat) differs from Mark's (unshrunk cloth); see the note.

settings.what: Parable of new wine and old wineskins
settings.to: The same critics
settings.when: Continuing the answer about fasting
settings.why: To make the same point with wine: fermenting new wine bursts old, stiff skins. The life Jesus brings needs new forms, or both the wine and the skins are lost.
settings.readers: Luke's churches of Jews and Gentiles were still working out which Jewish practices to keep (Acts 15; 21:20–26); the sayings told them the new life needed its own forms.

settings.what: The saying about old wine
settings.to: The same critics
settings.when: At the end of the answer about fasting
settings.why: To name the reason many will reject the new: those who like the old do not want to try anything else. Jesus speaks with irony but also with understanding of how people cling to the familiar. Only Luke records the saying.
views: Most read it as a description of the critics' resistance.
Some read it as a word in favor of Jewish tradition.
